claim: Keep the base mesh lean (low-poly, few extra vertices) and rely on a Subdivision Surface modifier for final roundness/resolution control, rather than manually modeling rounded/beveled geometry into the base mesh by hand -- a hand-rounded base mesh is harder to edit later (any later change to the shape means dealing with the extra vertices the manual rounding already added), whereas a lean base mesh plus a SubSurf modifier lets you raise or lower the effective resolution non-destructively at any time.
supporting_evidence: Per the narration at 0:14-1:54: Andrew Price describes trying to "round everything by hand" without a SubSurf modifier as something that "creates a lot of problems" -- if you later want to change the shape you've "got all these extra vertices to deal with" -- versus keeping the mesh "lean" and adding SubSurf, which "gives you the control of ... how high resolution do you want the final model to be, you can just turn it up or down."
rejected_alternative: Deleting/avoiding the Subdivision Surface modifier and manually rounding sharp edges with hand geometry (e.g. a manual bevel) baked into the base mesh.

claim: For controlling how sharp a Subdivision-Surface-smoothed edge reads, this video explicitly rejects Edge Crease (Shift+E) as the primary tool, on the stated grounds that crease only behaves predictably at its maximum value -- intermediate crease values (e.g. 0.5) don't give reliable, controllable partial sharpness. The video's recommended alternative is adding loop cuts near the edge instead (a "support"/"proximity" loop), which gives continuous, predictable control over apparent sharpness by narrowing the span the modifier averages across.
supporting_evidence: Per the narration at 2:00-3:14: "the first way is one that i don't recommend, a lot of people say you should do it but doesn't really work, and that is to add a crease" -- demonstrated with Shift+E; at partial values ("say 0.5") he says "it's almost like it's not fully -- you don't have full control over this ... honestly like the crease generally whenever i use a crease it's just to make it maximum crease, it doesn't really work in the in between values."
rejected_alternative: Edge Crease (Shift+E) dragged to an intermediate value to get a partially-sharp, partially-smoothed edge.
reason: This directly bears on this project's unresolved bevel/SubD ordering contradiction: this source uses neither Bevel-before-SubD nor Bevel-after-SubD -- it doesn't use the Bevel modifier at all for edge sharpness. It's a third approach (support loops against plain SubD) and it specifically flags Edge Crease, a mechanism the project hasn't evaluated yet either, as unreliable outside its maximum setting. Worth weighing before trusting crease as a stand-in for bevel-weight in any future workflow.

claim: To sharpen a specific edge under a Subdivision Surface modifier without crease or bevel: add a loop cut (Ctrl+R) and slide it close to the target edge (a "support" or "proximity" loop). This shrinks the span of geometry the modifier averages across at that edge, making it read sharper. Adding a second loop cut even closer sharpens it further; sharpness is controlled by loop proximity/count, not a single sharpness parameter.
supporting_evidence: Per the narration at 3:47-5:05: "the reason that this is so smoothed out is because it is averaging out this huge area ... but watch this if we add a loop cut ... now it only has to go from there to there to there ... and if we want to smooth it even more, sharpen it even more, then we would add another loop cut" -- described as giving "the best of both worlds," full sharpness control plus a still-fairly-lean model.
rejected_alternative: Relying on Edge Crease for the same result (see the paired DECISION item on why crease was rejected here).

claim: Adding a loop cut intended to sharpen one local edge can unintentionally wrap all the way around a connected part of the mesh (e.g. around the entire horn of the anvil), creating an unwanted sharp edge somewhere else that the modeler didn't intend and may not notice until zooming out to see the whole model.
supporting_evidence: Per the narration at 11:19-12:03: "look at what we've done to our horn, our horn suddenly has something that we don't want ... this is a problem that i created deliberately because you come across this a lot ... you'll think like oh i need to add an edge loop here to sort of make this edge sharp but you don't realize that as you're hitting ctrl r and you pull it up, right, when you finally zoom out you realize that edge loop goes all the way around your model and now you've got a sharp edge where you didn't want there to be a sharp edge."

claim: To remove an unwanted portion of a sharpening loop cut without losing precise control of where the remaining sharp edge terminates: select the unwanted edge segment, press G twice (vertex/edge slide) to redirect it so it merges into an adjacent parallel loop, then Remove Doubles (merge by distance) to weld the coincident vertices, then fill any resulting small gap with F. This is preferred over simply dissolving/collapsing the unwanted edge because the slide-and-merge keeps the modeler in direct visual control of exactly where the loop is redirected to, rather than trusting an automatic dissolve/collapse operation to land it in the right place.
supporting_evidence: Per the narration at 12:52-15:17: "to select the edge that you want to move ... and then to double tap g and then pull it across ... and then if we were to remove the doubles ... we've got rid of that edge loop across the top there." On the suggested alternative (Dissolve Edge / Collapse Edge): "those did work for that situation, which is true, but for this specific situation we actually do want to do this because then we have an actual control over where this line actually goes."
rejected_alternative: Dissolve Edge or Collapse Edge on the unwanted loop segment.

claim: A patch of subsurf-smoothed mesh that looks noticeably more rounded/blobby than neighboring areas that already have support loops is the visual signal that a support loop is missing there -- the fix is to add a loop cut in that area to match the sharpness of the surrounding geometry.
supporting_evidence: Per the narration at 10:47-10:58: "now it's looking pretty good but you can see that this area here is really rounded because we haven't got that loop cut like we had here."
